claims.text: High-temperature service exposure promotes formation of fine intermetallic precipitates in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The resulting intermetallic precipitates pin dislocations and thereby improve mechanical strength.
The precipitates produce localized lattice mismatch that alters thermoelastic response.
The initial as-cast or homogenized alloy has no significant secondary-phase formation.
Aging at 1000°C for 10 hours in an inert atmosphere can drive precipitation.
The precipitates form both along grain boundaries and within grains.
The precipitates restrict dislocation mobility by acting as pinning centers.
Lattice mismatch between the precipitates and matrix causes local variations in elastic moduli.
The combined dislocation-pinning and lattice-mismatch effects modulate mechanical and thermoelastic performance.
Relative to an untreated sample, the aged alloy will have a statistically measurable increase in yield strength.
Relative to an untreated sample, the aged alloy will exhibit a distinct shift in thermoelastic modulus.
Changes in strength and thermoelastic modulus will correlate with precipitate morphology and density.
The proposed precipitation mechanism applies when oxidation is minimized and the exposure is sufficient for precipitation without excessive grain growth or competing transformations.
Precipitation kinetics, morphology, and thermoelastic effects vary with alloy composition and processing history.
Samples from the same batch can be divided into an aged group and an unchanged control group for subsequent mechanical and microstructural comparison.
